newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan shocked by miscues in nuclear accident.
newsitem.headline: Japan shocked by miscues in nuclear accident.

text.p: Japan reacted with shock and anger on Thursday to details emerging on the country's worst atomic accident which showed lengthy delays in notifying residents of the crisis and outdated firefighting equipment.

The 37 workers exposed to mild radiation during a fire and explosion on Tuesday at the Tokaimura nuclear reprocessing plant were given a clean bill of health, but for the state-run plant's operators there was no escaping the publicity fallout.

Politicians and nuclear safety officials joined the media in subjecting the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), to withering criticism for mishandling a potential disaster just 160 km (100 miles) from Tokyo.

The PNC was flailed for a lax reaction to the fire, ageing fire equipment and delays in informing local and national authorities, including Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who all learned first of the accident from television.

"If this tepid response reflects its best efforts in the disclosure and dissemination of information, the PNC's idiosyncratic mindset is hopeless," said the liberal daily newspaper Asahi Shimbun in an editorial.
Government officials revealed that Hashimoto, who the day after the accident formally apologised to the nation in parliament, learned of the explosion two and a half hours after it happened.

The accident, in which a fire that caused radiation to escape was not extinguished properly, triggering an explosion 10 hours later, came as the PNC was already reeling from an accident and cover-up at the Monju prototype fast-breeder reactor in December 1995.
In the Monju coverup, officials tried to hide a video showing that an accident in a coolant plant, which has shut the facility, was more serious than they reported.

"The lessons of Monju were not well taken," admitted Hiroto Ishida, the most senior bureaucrat at the Science and Technology Agency, which oversees the PNC. "How can I apologise enough?" he told a news conference.
Ishida's question is likely to be repeated frequently throughout the PNC, a key unit of resource-poor Japan's ambitious nuclear power programme.
Newspaper savagely revealed a list of miscues in handling the crisis in the plant's bitumisation facility.
There was no fulltime plant employee on duty when the accident happened, with a junior staff member from a subcontractor left to run the firefighting operation.
Newspapers said the officer wasted time in reacting to the blaze by awaiting telephone orders from the PNC's main security officer.
Further time was lost because the sprinkler in the burning facility was a manual system which required workers to turn on water taps by hand.
Smoke and heat sensors in the plant shut off after the first fire and were unable to give a warning that the blaze was still smouldering out of sight, leading to the later explosion.
Local officials were incensed that plant officials never once alerted residents, including schools and an old people's home just three km (1.8 miles) from the complex.
Atsuyuki Suzuki, professor of nuclear engineering at Tokyo University, called the accident a technological as well as a political blow to Japan's nuclear industry.
"PNC's research plans will face new scrutiny and scepticism about technical feasibility," Suzuki told Reuters. "What the nuclear industry thought could never happen has happened."
